name: Artificial Peace
label: Dischord
lede: Four kids from Bethesda pulled one of the biggest crowds in early DC hardcore, recorded 17 songs in a single Inner Ear session, and broke up with three of them on Flex Your Head. The other 14 waited until 2010.

eras.title: Bethesda shows up
eras.text: Artificial Peace came out of the Maryland suburbs, tight, fast and aggressive. By Dischord's account they drew one of the largest followings of any early DC band, and they were among the first from the area to play outside it.

years.h: Red C's guitarist meets three-fourths of Assault and Battery
years.p: Guitarist [[Pete Murray|6ab4a566-a279-441a-af5f-4d47459e1c18]] comes over from Red C. Singer [[Steve Polcari|33611a9d-0a07-418b-ac27-b51a58f93561]], bassist [[Rob Moss|3ff1431f-c33e-47f4-80ae-df8c0ba0d7fb]] and drummer [[Mike Manos|2da8a8ac-dab6-4b39-9ca6-ce91fee93fcf]] bring what's left of Assault and Battery.

years.cap: Flier for Artificial Peace's show of January 9, 1982
years.h: Bethesda's loudest export plays out of town
years.p: Dischord remembers Artificial Peace as one of the most followed early DC bands, and among the first from the area to play beyond it. Out of town, they made a point of saying they were from Bethesda.
years.xp:
A live recording from the Wilson Center on September 21, 1981 circulates on YouTube, audio only.

The UMD Persistent Vision archive holds several Artificial Peace fliers from 1982, drawn from the Sharon Cheslow Punk Flyers collection.

eras.title: Flex Your Head, then done
eras.text: Flex Your Head put Artificial Peace in the first document of DC hardcore just as the band was ending. Within a year Polcari, Murray and Manos had started Marginal Man, and Moss was touring with Government Issue.

years.h: Three songs on Flex Your Head, then the first 4,000 sell out
years.p: "Artificial Peace", "Outside Looking In" and "Wasteland" come from the November 1981 Inner Ear session and land on Dischord No. 7. Wikipedia says the first 4,000 copies were gone within a week.
years.xp: Dischord lists the band's tracks as release 007.8, a slice of the compilation that put DC hardcore on one record. The rest of the 17-song session stayed on tape until 2010.

years.h: A split 7" with the Exiled on Fountain of Youth
years.p: The only vinyl of its own that Artificial Peace put out while together.

years.cap: Flier for the June 25, 1982 Wilson Center show, taped and released in 2022
years.h: Artificial Peace ends and Marginal Man starts
years.p: Polcari, Murray and Manos add [[Kenny Inouye|a2ae807d-953b-496b-ac75-62d55c5f0afc]] and [[Andre Lee|b9484df3-7dce-4c9b-be55-072f26ca9498]] and start [[Marginal Man|fff14e91-ae03-4105-8fbb-3a318d6c01ca]], one of DC's first two-guitar hardcore bands.

years.h: Moss takes the bass to Government Issue
years.p: The former Artificial Peace bassist goes on the road with [[Government Issue|9b952ee8-d45d-4a26-8066-57849d871e06]] in 1983.

eras.title: The vault opens
eras.text: Nearly three decades on, Dischord put out the whole November 1981 session, and a live tape from 1982 followed. For a band known by three songs, it was the first full picture.

years.h: All 17 songs finally come out, 29 years late
years.p: In November 1981 [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] recorded Artificial Peace's entire set at Inner Ear. Only three songs came out while the band lasted; Dischord released the lot in 2010 as No. 167.
years.xp:
The session runs from "Suburban Wasteland" and "UXB" to "Spook Surf" and "This Means War". Dischord's notes call Artificial Peace one of the leading bands in the DC hardcore scene at the time. The 2010 LP was mastered at Chicago Mastering Service and pressed on translucent orange vinyl.

One of the three songs released in the band's lifetime was "Outside Looking In". Steve Polcari later used that phrase to explain the name of his next band, [[Marginal Man|fff14e91-ae03-4105-8fbb-3a318d6c01ca]].

years.h: A Wilson Center tape from 1982 turns up as a record
years.p: Artificial Peace's June 25, 1982 set at DC's Wilson Center was taped and shelved. Alona's Dream Records released it in 2022 as Live At The Wilson Center | June 25, 1982, 40 years later.
